guide.summary: Unit 1 introduces the rhetorical situation (exigence, writer, audience, purpose, context, message) and the basic building blocks of argument: claims and the evidence that supports them. You will learn to read a nonfiction text by asking why the writer made each choice for this audience, and to answer the exam's two kinds of multiple-choice questions: reading questions about published-style texts and writing questions that revise a student draft.

sections.heading: The rhetorical situation: six parts, one question
sections.body:
Every AP Lang reading question, and the whole rhetorical analysis essay, rests on one idea: a writer makes choices to accomplish a purpose with a particular audience in a particular context. The CED breaks this **rhetorical situation** into parts you should be able to name for any text:

| Part | Ask | Example (a principal's speech reopening a library) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exigence | What prompted this text, right now? | The library nearly closed; now it is reopening. |
| Writer/speaker | Who is speaking, and what is their relationship to the audience? | The principal who announced the closure. |
| Audience | Who is addressed? What do they believe, value, need? | Parents, some of whom heard the first announcement. |
| Purpose | What does the writer want the audience to think, feel, or do? | Accept the reversal and trust the school's promise. |
| Context | Time, place, and circumstances around the text. | A school deciding how to spend scarce space. |
| Message | The main idea the writer communicates. | Usage data missed what the library really offers. |

The question behind all of this: **why would this writer make this choice for this audience at this moment?** If you can answer that, you can answer most "primarily serves to" questions, because the right answer always connects a detail to the purpose or audience.

*Annotated example.* A speaker begins: "Three years ago, I stood in this room and told a group of parents—some of you were here—that the library would close." The aside "some of you were here" is not filler. It reminds part of the audience that they witnessed the original decision, which makes the speaker's later admission of error more honest and more personal.

sections.heading: The writer's relationship to the audience
sections.body:
Writers adjust to what an audience already believes. The CED calls this demonstrating an understanding of the audience's **beliefs, values, or needs**. Common moves:

- **Building credibility (ethos)** by admitting a limitation, citing experience, or showing fairness to the other side. A writer who says "I was wrong" before explaining why gains trust from listeners who heard the original claim.
- **Finding common ground** with shared values ("we all want our children to have somewhere to think").
- **Anticipating objections** the audience is likely to raise.
- **Choosing evidence the audience will accept.** A city council worried about budgets responds to cost figures; a congregation might respond to moral appeals.

On the exam you will rarely be asked to label something "ethos" or "pathos." Instead you will be asked what a choice does: "establishes the speaker's credibility," "anticipates a likely objection," "appeals to the audience's sense of responsibility." Learn to describe the effect in plain words.

*Annotated example.* "I will not embarrass her by name, though she is sitting in the third row and knows exactly who she is." Humor, warmth, and a public acknowledgment all at once. The speaker is showing parents that the decision was reversed because the school listened to a student, which is something parents value.

sections.heading: Claims and evidence
sections.body:
A **claim** is an arguable statement that requires support. A **thesis** is the main claim of the whole text; body paragraphs make supporting claims. **Evidence** is what supports a claim: facts, statistics, examples, anecdotes, expert testimony, personal experience, analogies, and details from texts.

Exam questions in this area ask you to:

1. Identify the claim a paragraph makes, especially when it is implied rather than stated.
2. Describe the type of evidence and its function ("provides an example that illustrates...", "offers data that challenges...").
3. Judge whether evidence is relevant and sufficient for the claim. Evidence can be accurate and still be the wrong evidence for the question being asked.

That third point is a favorite of exam writers. In the library speech, the principal's circulation numbers "were accurate," but they measured books borrowed, not the library's real use. Expect questions where the right answer separates *accuracy* from *relevance*.

**Writing-side questions** flip this around. You are given a student draft and asked which added sentence "best supports the claim in sentence 6." The right choice must (a) be about the same claim, (b) actually support it, and (c) fit the draft's audience and scope. A vivid but off-topic statistic is wrong; a relevant but weak anecdote usually loses to relevant data that generalizes.

sections.heading: How the multiple-choice section uses these skills
sections.body:
The MCQ section has two kinds of sets.

**Reading sets** (two sets, 23–25 questions in all) give you a nonfiction passage, often a speech, essay, or letter, sometimes from the 18th or 19th century, and ask how parts of it work. Stems look like:

- "The primary purpose of the passage is to..."
- "In the context of the passage as a whole, paragraph 3 functions to..."
- "The writer's reference to X serves mainly to..."
- "The speaker's attitude toward Y can best be described as..."

**Writing sets** (three sets, 20–22 questions in all) give you a student draft with numbered sentences and ask you to revise it. Stems look like:

- "The writer wants to add a sentence to provide evidence for the claim in sentence 4. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?"
- "The writer is considering deleting sentence 9. Should the writer keep or delete it?"
- "Which version of sentence 10 (reproduced below) best...?" with "(as it is now)" as option A.

Every writing question names a **goal**. Read the goal twice and choose the option that accomplishes exactly that goal. Correct grammar and pleasant style are necessary but never enough.

Each question has **four** answer choices (changed from five beginning with the 2025 exam).

sections.heading: Reading strategy that works under time pressure
sections.body:
1. **Read the italic introduction first.** It gives the writer, audience, date, and occasion, which is most of the rhetorical situation for free.
2. **Read the passage once for purpose.** At the end of each paragraph, jot a three-word label ("admits mistake," "numbers ≠ use," "student's tally").
3. **Predict before you look.** For a "serves to" question, reread the cited lines plus a sentence on either side, then say in your own words what the line does. Then match.
4. **Eliminate with the passage, not with your opinion.** Wrong choices usually (a) contradict the text, (b) go too far ("always," "entirely," "abolish"), (c) describe something that happens elsewhere in the passage, or (d) are true but do not answer the question.
5. **For keep/delete questions**, decide keep or delete first, then pick the reason that is actually true.

sections.heading: From reading to writing: the rhetorical analysis essay
sections.body:
Unit 1 also launches the rhetorical analysis essay (FRQ 2). The prompt is stable: *analyze the rhetorical choices the writer makes to convey a message/achieve a purpose.* A strong essay:

- Opens with the **rhetorical situation** in a sentence or two (who, to whom, when, why).
- States a **thesis** that names the writer's purpose and the main choices that serve it. Weak: "The speaker uses imagery, humor, and repetition." Strong: "By ranking machines against human eyes and comparing the landscape to a memorized sentence, the speaker convinces trainees that their small, unglamorous job is irreplaceable."
- Builds **body paragraphs around choices**, each with quoted evidence and two to three sentences of commentary explaining *how* the choice affects *this* audience.
- Treats the passage as a sequence: what does the writer do first, then why shift?

Commentary is where the 4 points in Row B live. A useful test: if you deleted your quotation, would your sentence still say something about the writer's purpose? If not, you are summarizing.

keyTakeaways: Every choice in a text is explained by the rhetorical situation: exigence, writer, audience, purpose, context, message.
Evidence can be accurate but irrelevant; questions often hinge on whether evidence fits the claim being made.
Revision questions always state a goal; the correct choice accomplishes that goal in that location.
Describe effects in plain language ("builds credibility by admitting error") instead of labeling appeals.
In rhetorical analysis, the thesis must link the writer's choices to a purpose; listing devices earns no credit.
commonMistakes: Picking an answer that is true about the passage but does not answer the question asked.
Choosing extreme answers ("abolish," "entirely," "contemptuous") when the passage is measured.
Keeping a sentence in a draft because it is interesting rather than because it advances the argument.
Writing commentary that paraphrases the quotation instead of explaining its effect on the audience.
Ignoring the italic introduction, which often states the audience and occasion.
examTips: Expect 1–3 questions per reading set on purpose or function of a paragraph, sentence, or detail.
Writing sets include add/delete, evidence selection, and audience-targeting questions; option A is often "(as it is now)" and is correct about as often as any other choice.
On "best supports the claim" questions, prefer evidence that is both relevant and generalizable (data or a representative example) over a vivid but narrow anecdote.
For the rhetorical analysis essay, name the audience in your thesis or opening; Row C often rewards explaining why a choice fits this specific situation.
Budget about 80 seconds per MCQ; reading passages take longer up front, so move quickly through revision items.
guide.cramSheet:
**Rhetorical situation:** exigence, writer, audience, purpose, context, message. Ask: why this choice, for this audience, now?

**Claim vs. evidence:** claim = arguable; evidence = facts, data, examples, anecdotes, testimony. Accurate ≠ relevant.

**Reading stems:** "primarily serves to," "functions to," "purpose," "attitude." Predict, then match. Eliminate extreme, contradicted, or elsewhere-in-passage choices.

**Writing stems:** goal stated in stem → choose the option that does exactly that job. Keep/delete: decide first, then pick the true reason.

**Credibility moves:** admitting error, citing experience, fairness to opponents, shared values.

**FRQ 2 thesis formula:** In [context], [writer] [verbs: argues/urges/reassures] [audience] that [message] by [choice 1] and [choice 2].

**Row B:** commentary > quotation. **Row C:** explain why the choices fit this situation, or the tension the writer manages.

**MCQ:** 45 questions, 60 minutes, four choices each.

vocab.definition: The set of circumstances a text responds to: exigence, writer, audience, purpose, context, and message.
The problem, event, or need that prompts a writer to write at a particular moment.
vocab.example: A city council vote on closing branch libraries is the exigence for a librarian's op-ed.

vocab.definition: The specific people a writer addresses, whose beliefs, values, and needs shape the writer's choices.
What the writer wants the audience to understand, feel, believe, or do.
The time, place, and circumstances surrounding a text, including cultural and historical conditions.
The main idea a writer communicates; in an argument, closely tied to the thesis.
An arguable statement that requires support with evidence and reasoning.
The overarching claim of an argument, which the rest of the text supports; may preview the argument's structure.
Information used to support a claim: facts, statistics, examples, anecdotes, expert testimony, or textual details.
A brief story used as evidence or to engage the audience; persuasive emotionally but usually limited in how far it generalizes.
The audience's trust in the writer, built through expertise, fairness, honesty, or shared values.
A choice that moves the audience by engaging feelings such as sympathy, fear, or pride.
A choice that persuades through reasoning, data, and evidence.
Acknowledging that an opposing point has some validity, often before rebutting it.
A response that answers or refutes an opposing claim.
Whether evidence actually bears on the specific claim it is meant to support.
Whether there is enough evidence, of the right kind, to justify a claim.
The writer's explanation of how evidence supports a claim; in essays, the analysis that connects quotation to argument.

practice.stimulus:
The following passage is from a speech given by a high school principal to parents at the reopening of a renovated school library that had nearly been converted into a computer lab. (Original passage written for practice.)

(1) Three years ago, I stood in this room and told a group of parents—some of you were here—that the library would close. I said it the way administrators say such things: the numbers did not justify the space. Circulation had fallen by half in a decade. The encyclopedias had not been opened in years, and our students, we were told, did their research on their phones. I believed every word I said. I was also wrong.

(2) I was not wrong about the numbers. The numbers were accurate. I was wrong about what they measured. Circulation counts the books that leave a building. It does not count the sophomore who stays until six because the apartment she goes home to has eleven people in it. It does not count the boy who reads the same graphic novel four times at the corner table because no one there asks him why he is not at practice. It does not count the quiet. And quiet, it turns out, is something many of our students cannot find anywhere else.

(3) I learned this the way I learn most things worth knowing: from a student who was annoyed with me. A junior—I will not embarrass her by name, though she is sitting in the third row and knows exactly who she is—came to my office with a clipboard. She had spent two weeks standing at the library door with a tally sheet. Not counting books, she said; counting people, and asking each one what they had come for. Four hundred and twelve visits in ten school days. Almost none of them, she pointed out, would appear in any report I had ever read.

(4) Her clipboard did not prove that the library should stay open. It proved something more modest and more important: that I had been answering a question no one had asked. I had asked, "Do students still borrow books?" She asked, "Where do students go when they need to think?" Those are different questions, and they lead to different rooms.

(5) So here is the room. You will notice there are fewer shelves than before and more tables. You will notice the encyclopedias are gone—I am not sentimental about everything. But the doors now open at seven and close at six, and by the entrance hangs a sign one of our art students painted. It says simply, "You may stay." I would ask every parent here to read it twice: once as an invitation to your children, and once as a promise from us.
practice.stem: The principal's primary purpose in the passage is to

choices.text: explain why an earlier decision to close the library was reversed and invite parents to value the renovated space
apologize to parents for the cost of renovating the library
argue that schools should stop collecting circulation statistics
praise a student for challenging school rules

practice.explanation: The speech recounts the original decision (paragraph 1), explains what the principal misjudged (2–4), and ends by presenting the room and its promise to parents (5). B captures both the explanation and the invitation.

distractors.C: The principal says the numbers were accurate; he questions what they measure, not whether to collect them.
distractors.D: The student collected data and was 'annoyed,' but she broke no rules, and praising her is a means, not the purpose.

practice.stem: In paragraph 2, the repeated phrase "It does not count" primarily serves to

choices.text: show that the circulation numbers were inaccurate
criticize the librarians for careless record-keeping
list kinds of library use that circulation data overlook
suggest that students were misusing the library

practice.explanation: Each sentence beginning "It does not count" names a use of the library (staying late, rereading, seeking quiet) that a count of borrowed books cannot capture.

distractors.A: The principal explicitly says "The numbers were accurate."
distractors.B: No one is blamed; the limitation is in the measure, not the staff.
distractors.D: The uses described are presented sympathetically.

practice.stem: The sentences "I believed every word I said. I was also wrong." (paragraph 1) function mainly to

choices.text: signal that the rest of the speech will defend the original decision
suggest that the parents present three years ago had been deliberately misled
introduce a digression about the unreliability of administrators
establish the speaker's credibility by admitting a mistake before presenting what changed his mind

practice.explanation: The short, blunt admission makes the principal appear honest and sets up the rest of the speech as an account of how he learned he was wrong. Admitting error to an audience that heard the original announcement builds ethos.

distractors.A: The speech explains why the decision was reversed, not defended.
distractors.B: "I believed every word" rules out deliberate deception.
distractors.C: The speech stays on the library; the self-description in paragraph 1 is brief and leads directly to the main point.

practice.stem: The distinction in paragraph 2 between being wrong "about the numbers" and wrong "about what they measured" is significant because it

choices.text: implies that the parents had misunderstood the original announcement
concedes that the original evidence was accurate while challenging its relevance to the decision
shows that the principal had relied on no evidence at all
reveals that the circulation statistics had been miscalculated

practice.explanation: The principal keeps the data ("The numbers were accurate") but argues they answered the wrong question: borrowing is not the same as using the library. That is a concession about accuracy paired with a challenge about relevance.

distractors.C: He relied on circulation data; the problem is what the data captured.
distractors.D: Directly contradicted by "The numbers were accurate."

choices.text: protect the student's privacy because her findings were controversial
express the principal's lingering irritation at being corrected
acknowledge the student's role with warmth and humor in front of an audience that includes her
suggest that the student exaggerated the results of her survey

practice.explanation: The aside is playful: it refuses to name her while all but pointing to her. It recognizes her contribution publicly and lightens the tone of the speech for the parents in the room.

distractors.B: It was the student who was "annoyed"; the principal's tone is affectionate.
distractors.D: Her numbers are reported without doubt and drive the reversal.
distractors.A: He effectively identifies her, so privacy is not the aim, and nothing suggests controversy.

practice.stem: The student's evidence described in paragraph 3 differs from the evidence the principal originally relied on chiefly in that it

choices.text: included visitors from outside the school
covered a longer period than the circulation figures did
came from a published report rather than from observation
recorded visits and their purposes rather than items borrowed

practice.explanation: Circulation counted books leaving the building; the student counted "people" and asked "what they had come for." The difference is in what was measured.

distractors.B: Ten school days is far shorter than a decade of circulation data.

(4) Her clipboard did not prove that the library should stay open. It proved something more modest and more important: that I had been answering a question no one had asked. I had asked, "Do students still borrow books?" She asked, "Where do students go when they need to think?" Those are different questions, and they lead to different rooms.

(5) So here is the room. You will notice there are fewer shelves than before and more tables. You will notice the encyclopedias are gone—I am not sentimental about everything. But the doors now open at seven and close at six, and by the entrance hangs a sign one of our art students painted. It says simply, "You may stay." I would ask every parent here to read it twice: once as an invitation to your children, and once as a promise from us.
practice.stem: In paragraph 4, the principal says the student's clipboard proved "something more modest and more important" than that the library should stay open. This characterization most strongly suggests that the principal

choices.text: holds that modest claims are always more persuasive than ambitious ones
values the student's reframing of the question more than any power her data had to settle the issue by itself
believes the student's data were too limited to be trusted
wants to minimize the student's contribution to the decision

practice.explanation: "More modest": the tally alone could not decide the library's future. "More important": it revealed that the principal had been asking the wrong question. The emphasis falls on the new question in the rest of the paragraph ("Where do students go when they need to think?"), so the reframing is what he values most.

distractors.A: Overgeneralizes a judgment about one piece of evidence into a universal rule.
distractors.D: Calling her finding "more important" elevates, rather than minimizes, her contribution.
distractors.C: He calls the proof modest in scope, not untrustworthy, and the data are accepted.

practice.stimulus:
The following passage is from a speech given by a high school principal to parents at the reopening of a renovated school library that had nearly been converted into a computer lab. (Original passage written for practice.)

(1) Three years ago, I stood in this room and told a group of parents—some of you were here—that the library would close. I said it the way administrators say such things: the numbers did not justify the space. Circulation had fallen by half in a decade. The encyclopedias had not been opened in years, and our students, we were told, did their research on their phones. I believed every word I said. I was also wrong.

(2) I was not wrong about the numbers. The numbers were accurate. I was wrong about what they measured. Circulation counts the books that leave a building. It does not count the sophomore who stays until six because the apartment she goes home to has eleven people in it. It does not count the boy who reads the same graphic novel four times at the corner table because no one there asks him why he is not at practice. It does not count the quiet. And quiet, it turns out, is something many of our students cannot find anywhere else.

(3) I learned this the way I learn most things worth knowing: from a student who was annoyed with me. A junior—I will not embarrass her by name, though she is sitting in the third row and knows exactly who she is—came to my office with a clipboard. She had spent two weeks standing at the library door with a tally sheet. Not counting books, she said; counting people, and asking each one what they had come for. Four hundred and twelve visits in ten school days. Almost none of them, she pointed out, would appear in any report I had ever read.

(4) Her clipboard did not prove that the library should stay open. It proved something more modest and more important: that I had been answering a question no one had asked. I had asked, "Do students still borrow books?" She asked, "Where do students go when they need to think?" Those are different questions, and they lead to different rooms.

(5) So here is the room. You will notice there are fewer shelves than before and more tables. You will notice the encyclopedias are gone—I am not sentimental about everything. But the doors now open at seven and close at six, and by the entrance hangs a sign one of our art students painted. It says simply, "You may stay." I would ask every parent here to read it twice: once as an invitation to your children, and once as a promise from us.
practice.stem: The principal's request that parents read the sign "twice" (paragraph 5) primarily serves to

choices.text: turn a message addressed to students into a commitment the school makes to families, ending the speech with a pledge
imply that parents had failed to read earlier school communications carefully
suggest that the sign's wording is ambiguous and needs further explanation
draw attention to the artistic skill of the student who painted it

practice.explanation: Read once, "You may stay" invites students; read again "as a promise from us," it binds the school to keep the doors open. The double reading converts the room's purpose into an obligation to the audience of parents, a fitting close after a speech about a reversed decision.

distractors.B: Nothing in the speech accuses parents of inattention.
distractors.C: The principal explains both readings himself; he is not flagging confusion.
distractors.D: The painter is mentioned, but the request concerns what the words mean to parents, not the artistry.

practice.stimulus:
The following is a draft of a student's opinion essay for the school newspaper. (Original passage written for practice.)

(1) In the past five years, more than a dozen "community fridges"—refrigerators placed on sidewalks and stocked by neighbors with free food—have appeared in our city. (2) Anyone may take what they need, and anyone may leave what they can spare. (3) Critics say the fridges are unsanitary and attract litter. (4) These concerns are not imaginary. (5) A fridge on Alder Street was removed last spring after a resident complained about spoiled milk that had been left inside for days. (6) But the solution to a poorly maintained fridge is maintenance, not removal. (7) The volunteer group that runs the Fifth Avenue fridge, for example, checks it twice a day and keeps a log of every item it discards. (8) Since adopting the log in 2021, the group has received no health complaints. (9) My grandmother, who lived through the Great Depression, always kept extra food in the house. (10) The city should therefore support community fridges by creating a simple registration system that requires each fridge to have a named volunteer team and a cleaning schedule.
practice.stem: The writer is considering deleting sentence 9. Should the writer keep or delete this sentence?

choices.text: Keep, because it gives historical context about food insecurity in the city
Keep, because it establishes the writer's personal authority on food storage
Delete, because it contradicts the claim made in sentence 6
Delete, because it introduces a personal detail that does not advance the argument about maintaining and regulating the fridges

practice.explanation: Sentences 6–8 argue that maintenance solves the sanitation problem and sentence 10 proposes a registration system. A grandmother's habit of storing food does not support either claim and interrupts the line of reasoning.

distractors.A: The sentence concerns one household during the Depression, not food insecurity in the city.
distractors.B: A relative's habit gives the writer no authority on the issue.
distractors.C: It does not contradict sentence 6; it is simply irrelevant.

choices.text: Electric refrigerators first became common in American homes in the 1920s and 1930s.

In sentence 4 (reproduced below), the writer wants to concede the critics' point while signaling that the essay will go on to answer it.

These concerns are not imaginary.

Which version of sentence 4 best accomplishes this goal?

choices.text: These concerns are not imaginary, though they point to a problem with upkeep rather than with the fridges themselves.
(as it is now)
These concerns are entirely accurate, which is why some fridges have been removed.
These concerns, however, are rarely raised by people who actually use the fridges.

practice.explanation: The correct version grants the concern ("not imaginary") and, with "though," signals the rebuttal the essay develops in sentence 6: the issue is upkeep, not the fridges.

practice.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 7 and 8 to make clear the relationship between the group's routine and the result. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

choices.text: The volunteer group that runs the Fifth Avenue fridge checks it twice a day and keeps a log of every item it discards, and the group has received no health complaints.
Since 2021, when the volunteer group that runs the Fifth Avenue fridge began logging every item it discards during its twice-daily checks, the group has received no health complaints.
The volunteer group that runs the Fifth Avenue fridge has received no health complaints, checking it twice a day and logging items since 2021.
Although the volunteer group that runs the Fifth Avenue fridge checks it twice a day and logs discarded items, it has received no health complaints since 2021.

practice.explanation: The correct choice subordinates the routine to a "Since..., when..." clause, so the result (no complaints) is presented as following from the logging practice, preserving the 2021 date and the twice-daily checks.

distractors.A: "And" merely adds the two facts side by side without showing that one led to the other.
distractors.C: The participial phrase is loosely attached and blurs which action began in 2021.
distractors.D: "Although" signals contrast, implying the result is surprising given the routine, which reverses the logic.

The writer wants to add the following sentence to the passage.

Spoiled food is a real hazard, and no one is helped by a fridge that makes people sick.

Where would the sentence best be placed?

After sentence 5

practice.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 10 so that the proposal is more likely to persuade city council members who worry about the cost of new programs. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

practice.stimulus:
The following passage is from a talk given by a retired fire lookout to new seasonal lookouts at the start of their training. Lookouts spend the summer alone in towers on mountain peaks, watching for smoke. (Original passage written for practice.)

You have been told that satellites and cameras will do most of your job. That is partly true. A satellite will find a fire the size of a parking lot. A camera on a ridge will find a fire the size of a house, if the light is right and the wind is not. You will find the fire the size of a campfire—a gray thread at four in the afternoon that might be dust, might be cloud, might be nothing. That thread is why you are here. Fires the size of parking lots are already expensive. Fires the size of campfires are still cheap.

Here is what nobody tells you about watching. It is not looking. Looking is what you do for the first week, when you scan the horizon every fifteen minutes because the manual says to and you are proud of yourself for remembering. Watching begins later, around the third week, when the horizon stops being scenery and becomes a sentence you have memorized. You know which canyon breathes fog at dawn. You know the logging road that throws dust when the trucks run on Tuesdays. And one afternoon something on that sentence is misspelled, and you see it before you know you have seen it.

I will not pretend this is glamorous. You will eat a great deal of canned chili. You will talk to the ravens and, in a bad year, they will start to answer. You will read every book you brought by July and every label on every can by August. Some of you will decide by the Fourth of July that you are not made for this, and there is no shame in that. Solitude is a skill, not a virtue, and not everyone needs to learn it.

But for those of you who stay: the reward is not the view, although the view is very good. The reward is that for one summer of your life you will know a piece of the earth better than anyone alive knows it. You will be the expert on eleven hundred square miles of ridges and drainages, and the people in the valley—who will never learn your name—will sleep a little easier because you are awake.

So learn the sentence. Read it every morning. And when it changes, pick up the radio.
practice.prompt:
Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the retired lookout makes to convey his message to new seasonal lookouts.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
- Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
- Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
- Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

rubric.description: Responds to the prompt with a defensible thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices. 0 points for restating the prompt, summarizing the passage with no claim, or merely listing devices without saying what they accomplish.

4: Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning AND consistently explains how the evidence supports the line of reasoning AND explains how multiple rhetorical choices in the passage contribute to the writer's argument, purpose, or message. 3: Specific evidence supports all claims; explains how some evidence supports the line of reasoning and how at least one rhetorical choice contributes to the message. 2: Mix of specific evidence and generalities; explains some evidence but no line of reasoning is established, or explanation of rhetorical choices is faulty or listed rather than analyzed. 1: Mostly general evidence; commentary summarizes. 0: Simply restates the thesis or is incoherent. Errors that interfere with communication cap this row at 3.

Demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or a complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, for example by: Explaining the significance or relevance of the writer's rhetorical choices given the rhetorical situation; explaining a purpose or function of the passage's complexities or tensions; or employing a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive. It must be part of the argument, not a single phrase; sweeping openers ("Since the beginning of time...") and token concessions do not earn it.

practice.sampleResponse:
A speaker addressing new fire lookouts faces an odd rhetorical problem: his audience has already been told their job is nearly obsolete, and he knows that the loneliness of the job will drive some of them away. Rather than inflate the job, the retired lookout argues for its value by narrowing it. Through precise comparisons of scale, an extended metaphor of the landscape as a "sentence," and a deliberately unglamorous inventory of hardships, he persuades his listeners that their work is small, unromantic, and irreplaceable—and that this is exactly why it matters.

The speaker opens by conceding the point his audience has probably heard from everyone else: "That is partly true." Instead of arguing with the technology, he ranks it. A satellite finds "a fire the size of a parking lot," a camera "a fire the size of a house," and the lookout "the fire the size of a campfire." The descending scale does two things at once. It grants the machines real competence, which makes the speaker sound fair rather than nostalgic, and it carves out a space that only a human can fill. The final pair of short sentences converts that space into a practical argument: fires the size of parking lots are "already expensive," while campfires are "still cheap." For trainees who may suspect they are a budget line about to be cut, the speaker reframes their value in terms an agency would accept—cost—while also implying that their attention to tiny details is the most efficient firefighting there is.

Having established why a human is needed, the speaker turns to what the human must learn, and here his central choice is a metaphor. He distinguishes "looking," which is dutiful and self-congratulatory, from "watching," in which "the horizon stops being scenery and becomes a sentence you have memorized." The comparison is apt for an audience about to be alone with a single view for months: it tells them that the landscape will become legible, that boredom is the stage before fluency. His examples—the canyon that "breathes fog at dawn," the road that throws dust "on Tuesdays"—are so specific that they model the kind of knowledge he is describing. When he says that one day the sentence will be "misspelled" and "you see it before you know you have seen it," he gives the trainees something rarer than encouragement: a description of expertise from the inside, which they can recognize when it happens to them.

The third paragraph risks undercutting all of this, and that risk is deliberate. The canned chili, the ravens that "start to answer," the labels read by August: the humor is self-deprecating, and the list builds toward a frank admission that some of them "will decide by the Fourth of July" to leave. By saying there is "no shame in that" and that "solitude is a skill, not a virtue," the speaker earns credibility with the very people most likely to doubt him. He is not recruiting; he is telling the truth. That honesty makes the turn to "But for those of you who stay" more persuasive, because the reward he names afterward has survived his own skepticism.

The reward itself is framed in the same narrowing logic as the opening. It is "not the view," which a tourist could have, but knowledge "of a piece of the earth" deeper than anyone else's. The image of valley residents "who will never learn your name" sleeping "a little easier because you are awake" makes anonymity part of the honor: the job's invisibility is evidence of its success. The closing imperatives—"learn the sentence," "read it every morning," "pick up the radio"—return to the metaphor and compress the whole talk into a routine the trainees can follow on their first lonely morning.

What makes the speech effective is that its modesty is a strategy. An audience told that their job is heroic would discount the claim the first time the chili ran low. An audience told that their job is small, specific, and genuinely theirs has a reason to keep watching.
